```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_sqlite <- requireNamespace("DBI", quietly = TRUE) &&
  requireNamespace("RSQLite", quietly = TRUE)
```

groundplotqc checks any set of related tables against a specification you write. This
article runs the checks on a small fish survey: three tables of stations, hauls and catches.
It reads the survey's specification, checks its tables as data frames, then as CSV files and
from a database, and writes the results to a run folder.

## The specification

The specification is the survey's data dictionary, its code lists, its type map and its
missing-value codes, read as the article "Specification files and configuration" reads it.

```{r}
library(groundplotqc)
example <- function(file) system.file("extdata", "examples", file, package = "groundplotqc")
fish <- gpq_read_spec(
  dictionary = example("fish_dictionary.csv"),
  code_lists = list(
    water_body = example("fish_water_body.csv"), gear = example("fish_gear.csv"),
    species = example("fish_species.csv")
  ),
  column_map = gpq_column_map(
    table = "table", attribute = "field", type = "kind", key_type = "key",
    reference = "parent", lookup = "codes", description = "notes",
    min_value = "low", max_value = "high", min_inclusive = "low_in", max_inclusive = "high_in",
    pattern = "format", max_length = "width", decimals = "places", units = "unit"
  ),
  type_map = gpq_type_map(example("fish_types.csv")),
  sentinels = gpq_sentinels(
    numeric = c(missing = -99, not_applicable = -88),
    character = c(missing = "?", not_applicable = "~"),
    date = c(missing = "?", not_applicable = "~")
  )
)
```

## The tables as data frames

The tables are a named list, one data frame per table of the dictionary. This survey has two
mistakes: a catch whose weight is missing, written as `NA` where the specification's code for a
missing value is -99, and a gear code with a space after it.

```{r}
tables <- list(
  stations = data.frame(
    station_id = c("S1", "S2"), station_name = c("Long Lake", "Stony River"),
    water_body = c("LK", "RV"), depth = c(1.5, 2.5),
    first_visit = c("2020-06-01", "2020-06-02")
  ),
  hauls = data.frame(
    haul_id = c("H1", "H2", "H3"), station_id = c("S1", "S1", "S2"),
    gear = c("GN", "TN ", "EF"), minutes = c(30L, 45L, 20L),
    haul_date = c("2020-06-01", "2020-06-01", "2020-06-02")
  ),
  catches = data.frame(
    catch_id = c("C1", "C2", "C3", "C4"), haul_id = c("H1", "H1", "H2", "H3"),
    species = c("WAE", "NOP", "YEP", "LKT"), fish_count = c(3L, 1L, 4L, 2L),
    weight = c(1.2, 0.4, NA, 0.9)
  )
)
results <- gpq_check_conformance(tables, fish, group_cols = "water_body", layers = 0:2)
```

The results summary has one row for each rule, table, column and group. Each issue names
its rule, its record and the value that failed. The first table counts the summary's rows by
status; the open issues follow, each with its group column, `water_body`.

```{r}
table(results$results$status)
open <- results$issues[results$issues$status == "open", ]
open[, c("rule_id", "table_name", "column_name", "record_pk", "value", "water_body")]
```

One check doesn't run: `species_unknown_code` looks for the survey's codes for an unknown
species, and none are given, so it is recorded as not run, with the reason `no_input`. The
codes are given with the setting `unknown_codes` (see `?groundplotqc_options`).

## The tables as CSV files

The same tables can be given as paths of CSV files, here written to a temporary folder.
Every column of a CSV file is read as text, as written, so the checks of how a column is
stored don't run on it; they are recorded as not run, with the reason `text_input`.

```{r}
folder <- tempfile("fish")
dir.create(folder)
paths <- file.path(folder, paste0(names(tables), ".csv"))
names(paths) <- names(tables)
for (name in names(tables)) {
  data.table::fwrite(tables[[name]], paths[[name]])
}
from_csv <- gpq_check_conformance(paths, fish, group_cols = "water_body", layers = 0:2)
text_input <- from_csv$results$not_run_reason %in% "text_input"
from_csv$results[text_input, c("rule_id", "table_name", "column_name", "not_run_reason")]
```

The run's metadata records each file by its name and SHA-256, with its rows and the
separator that was found.

```{r, R.options = list(width = 125)}
from_csv$metadata$inputs
```

## The tables in a database

Tables in a database are read through a DBI connection. Where a table has another name in
the database, `table_map` gives it, such as `c(hauls = "survey.hauls")` for a table in the
schema survey. This part runs where the packages DBI and RSQLite are installed.

```{r, eval = has_sqlite, R.options = list(width = 125)}
connection <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
DBI::dbWriteTable(connection, "stations", tables$stations)
DBI::dbWriteTable(connection, "fish_hauls", tables$hauls)
DBI::dbWriteTable(connection, "fish_catches", tables$catches)
from_db <- gpq_check_conformance(
  connection, fish,
  table_map = c(hauls = "fish_hauls", catches = "fish_catches"),
  group_cols = "water_body", layers = 0:2
)
from_db$metadata$inputs
DBI::dbDisconnect(connection)
```

The database's tables give the same results as the data frames, and the metadata names each
table as the database names it, with the driver's class.

## The run folder

`gpq_write_results()` writes a run's results to a folder named by its run ID, and
`gpq_read_results()` reads them back.

```{r}
output <- tempfile("runs")
gpq_write_results(results, output)
run_dir <- file.path(output, results$metadata$run$run_id)
list.files(run_dir, recursive = TRUE)
again <- gpq_read_results(run_dir)
identical(again$issues, results$issues)
```

## Issue classes

Each issue has a class: `source`, for the provider to fix in their data; `harmonization`,
made when the data was converted to the specification's form; or `unclassified`.
`gpq_classify_issues()` gives each issue its rule's class, unless one of your overrides
gives it another. Where a rule's class is `depends`, the evidence you give can settle it,
and `class_basis` says what decided each issue's class.

Two more mistakes give the survey such issues: a station 600 metres deep, past the
dictionary's 500, and a haul of 900 minutes, past its 600. Both are `value_above_max`, a
rule whose class is `depends`.

```{r}
planted <- tables
planted$stations$depth[2] <- 600
planted$hauls$minutes[3] <- 900L
checked <- gpq_check_conformance(planted, fish, group_cols = "water_body", layers = 0:3)
```

An override records your decision: the long haul is the provider's to fix. A `computed`
row says the pipeline computes the stations' depth, so a wrong depth is harmonization. Its
column `water_body` is the run's group column, and `"*"` stands for every value.

```{r, R.options = list(width = 125)}
overrides <- data.frame(
  fingerprint = NA, rule_id = "value_above_max", table_name = "hauls",
  column_name = "minutes", issue_class = "source", who = "A. Reviewer",
  when = "2026-10-22", why = "The gear log gives 20 minutes."
)
computed <- data.frame(
  table_name = "stations", column_name = "depth", water_body = "*", derivation = "formula"
)
gpq_classify_issues(
  checked$issues,
  rules = NULL, evidence = list(computed = computed), overrides = overrides
)
checked$issues[, c("rule_id", "table_name", "column_name", "value", "issue_class", "class_basis")]
```

The other issues keep their rules' classes, with `class_basis` `default`. An issue whose
rule's class is `depends` and that nothing settles is `unclassified`; the setting
`fallback_class` gives such a rule a class of its own (see `?groundplotqc_options`).
